summary: Help 9-10 year olds classify 2-D figures by TESTING line properties (parallel sides, perpendicular sides, right angles in triangles) rather than sorting by overall appearance. The core skill is applying a reliable physical check — sliding or extending a ruler to confirm a constant gap for parallel lines, and using a set-square or the square corner of a card to confirm a 90 degree angle — and then sorting on the result. A single figure may carry more than one property (a rectangle has parallel sides AND right angles), so each property is decided by its own independent check. Two obstacles dominate: confusing the words 'parallel' and 'perpendicular', and treating non-defining features (unequal line length, or horizontal/vertical orientation) as if they decided the classification, because typical textbook pictures show equal-length parallel lines in standard orientation.
misconceptions: Confuses the vocabulary — mixes up 'parallel' and 'perpendicular'
Thinks parallel lines must be the same length (reinforced by always-equal-length textbook examples)
Only recognises parallel/perpendicular when the lines are horizontal or vertical; misses tilted pairs
Fails to recognise a right triangle when it is rotated or looks scalene (right-angle-legs prototype)

activities.title: Sort the tray: test every figure before you bin it
steps: Lay out a mixed tray of shapes and lines including a pair of parallel lines of clearly DIFFERENT lengths tilted off horizontal, a pair that looks parallel but slowly converges, a right-angled triangle rotated so neither leg is horizontal or vertical, a rectangle, and a non-right triangle.

For each pair of sides, test for parallel: slide a ruler along one side keeping it touching, and check whether the gap to the opposite side stays the same, measuring straight across (at right angles to the lines) at two or more places, including near both ends where the lines lie alongside each other, or extend both lines to see whether they would meet.
For each corner you suspect is a right angle, drop a set-square or the square corner of a card into the corner and check whether it fits exactly against both sides.

Record each figure by property, testing the two properties independently: does it have a pair of parallel sides? does it have a right angle / is it a right triangle? A figure may pass BOTH tests (a rectangle has parallel sides AND right angles), just one, or neither — note what each check shows rather than forcing it into a single exclusive box, and only decide after the check, not after a glance.

Say out loud, for at least three figures, which check you used and what it showed (for example: 'I slid the ruler and the gap never changed, so these sides are parallel even though one line is longer' or 'the rectangle passed both — parallel sides and a right-angle corner').
activities.insight: A property, not the look of a figure, decides the category: a tilted, unequal-length pair is just as parallel as a tidy horizontal pair, and a rotated triangle is still a right triangle if a corner tests at 90 degrees. Properties are independent, so a figure can have both (a rectangle), one, or neither. The question shifts from 'does it look like the book example?' to 'does it pass the test?'

activities.title: Draw it, don't just spot it
steps: Given a line drawn at an angle (not horizontal or vertical), draw a second line parallel to it, then check your own drawing by sliding a ruler to confirm the gap is constant.
Given another angled line, draw a line perpendicular to it, then check with a set-square or square corner that the crossing is a right angle.
Draw a right triangle that stands on its point or sits at an angle, so that neither of the two shorter sides is horizontal or vertical; mark the right angle and verify it with the set-square.
Swap drawings with a partner and test each other's lines and triangle with the ruler and set-square, reporting whether each one passes.
activities.insight: Producing parallel and perpendicular lines, and a right triangle in a non-standard orientation, is evidence the learner holds the defining property rather than copying a familiar picture.

activities.title: Sorting grids for mixed properties
steps: Set up a two-way sorting grid: one axis 'has parallel sides / no parallel sides', the other 'has a right angle / no right angle'.
Place each figure from a mixed set into the correct cell, including shapes that belong in the cell with BOTH parallel sides and a right angle (such as a rectangle).
For each placement, state the check you used and keep the ruler and set-square to hand so you can re-test any figure a classmate questions.
activities.insight: Properties combine: a figure can have parallel sides, a right angle, both, or neither, and each property is decided by its own independent check.

activities.title: Quick reference card for the two words
steps: Keep a small reference card where pointing to a pair of sides shows 'parallel: always the same distance apart, never meet' and pointing to a corner shows the 90 degree square for 'perpendicular / right angle'.
Use the card to settle vocabulary disputes during the sorting and drawing tasks, then return to the physical check to confirm the actual figure.
activities.insight: A quick visual anchor helps keep 'parallel' and 'perpendicular' straight, but naming is not the same as verifying — the figure in front of you still has to pass the ruler or set-square test.

checkQuestion: Put out a mixed set of shapes and lines. Include: (i) a pair of parallel lines of clearly DIFFERENT lengths, tilted off horizontal; (ii) a pair that looks parallel but slowly converges; (iii) a right-angled triangle rotated so neither leg is horizontal or vertical; and (iv) a rectangle and a non-right triangle. Give the child a set-square or the square corner of a card and say: 'Sort these — which have parallel sides, and which have a right angle or are right triangles — and show me how you check each one.' Say nothing about method; watch what they DO.
checkAnswer: The child uses a physical check — slides or extends lines to confirm two sides stay the same distance apart (parallel), and applies the set-square/paper corner to confirm a 90° angle — and sorts on the result: places the tilted, unequal-length pair with the parallels, rejects the slowly-converging pair, and identifies the rotated triangle as a right triangle regardless of its orientation.
